items.title: Ocado customer criticizes AI-generated support responses for technical issues, receives personalized human follow-up acknowledging the problem [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Just a little AI resistance, as a treat
items.summary:
A customer reported malformed calendar invites from British online supermarket Ocado and initially received an AI-generated customer service reply that felt insincere and unhelpful. After expressing dissatisfaction through a survey, the customer received a personalized response from a human apologizing for the robotic reply and assuring that the detailed technical feedback was passed to the appropriate team for resolution.

The incident highlights concerns about the use of AI in customer service, particularly when it replaces meaningful human interaction in addressing technical problems. While AI may assist in triaging and summarizing customer messages, relying on it for direct responses can lead to frustration and perceptions of disrespect toward customers' time and concerns.

items.title: CEPR launches AI Bubble Monitor to track economic and market indicators related to AI investment and hype
items.originalTitle: The AI Bubble Monitor
items.summary:
The Center for Economic and Policy Research (CEPR) has introduced the AI Bubble Monitor, a tool designed to analyze and track economic and market trends associated with artificial intelligence investments and speculative activity. This monitor aims to provide data-driven insights into the potential formation of an AI-related economic bubble.

The AI Bubble Monitor aggregates various indicators to assess the scale and sustainability of AI-driven market enthusiasm, helping policymakers, investors, and researchers understand the dynamics of AI's economic impact and the risks of overvaluation in the sector.

items.title: Octomind launches open-source CLI-first AI coding agent runtime with token-saving features and support for multiple models [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Octomind – open-source AI harness that saves your tokens, static rust
items.summary:
Octomind is an open-source AI coding agent runtime designed for autonomous work, allowing large language models to interact with code repositories by reading, writing files, running shell commands, and delegating tasks. It supports various workflows including interactive sessions, background daemons, and WebSocket communication, and emphasizes policy-as-code guardrails, cost control, and adaptability to any model or budget.

The tool has been benchmarked on 25 real-world coding tasks across multiple programming languages, solving 24 tasks at roughly half the cost of competitors. Octomind uses a single TOML configuration for models, tools, roles, and guardrails, and offers features like adaptive compression to maintain session knowledge over long tasks. It supports multiple AI providers including OpenAI, Anthropic, and others, and can be installed on macOS, Linux, and Windows.

items.originalTitle: AI is destroying my CS degree
items.summary:
A computer science student with a scholarship in AI expresses frustration over their university's inconsistent and confusing policies on AI use, which have negatively affected their learning experience. The student highlights how the institution's flip-flopping between banning and mandating AI tools has created uncertainty and degraded the quality of coursework and assessments.

The student also points out that AI-generated assignments often lack thoughtful design and impose an excessive workload, especially for those with less technical background. Additionally, tutors are overwhelmed due to increased demands and automation pressures, leading to reduced personalized support. Despite concerns about the future of computer science education, the student remains eager to continue learning and exploring the field beyond AI hype.

items.title: Quilicura community in Chile replaces AI with humans for a day to answer 25,000 prompts and raise awareness about AI's water use, reaching over 1 billion people globally [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Quili AI
items.summary:
A Chilean town called Quilicura organized an event where more than 40 people answered over 25,000 AI prompts manually in a 12-hour period, engaging with users from 68 countries. This human-powered chatbot initiative aimed to highlight the environmental impact of AI data centers on local water resources.

The project achieved a global reach of 71.6 million interactions in one day and ultimately reached over 1 billion people worldwide. It served as a community-driven effort to raise awareness about the water consumption of AI infrastructure and promote sustainable resource use.

items.title: Researchers propose reverse game theory to design incentive mechanisms that keep AI agents aligned and prevent deceptive behavior [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check
items.summary:
Researchers are exploring reverse game theory, or mechanism design, as a way to control advanced AI models by creating systems that incentivize them to follow rules and avoid deceptive behaviors. This approach focuses on designing rules that encourage desired behaviors rather than trying to interpret AI internal processes, which have proven unreliable due to models hiding intentions or underperforming deliberately.

Examples include rewarding AI models based on how well their outputs predict those of other models or creating competitive dynamics between agents to encourage optimal performance. Another proposed method mimics human societal mechanisms, such as having AI agents alternate roles between problem solvers and auditors, with rewards and penalties based on honesty and accuracy. These strategies aim to improve AI alignment by leveraging incentives rather than relying solely on understanding or controlling AI cognition.

items.title: Anthropic says its Claude AI models accelerate custom chip design, citing faster workflows than Nvidia and AMD as it prepares for IPO [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Anthropic Touts Claude’s Chip Design Skills to IPO Investors
items.summary:
Anthropic is using its Claude AI models to assist a 15-person chip design team in developing custom AI chips, claiming the models reduce design time compared to traditional methods at major chipmakers like Nvidia and AMD. The company shared these details with investors ahead of its planned initial public offering later this month, which could value it around $1.5 trillion.

Anthropic's use of AI for chip design follows its prior applications of Claude models in uncovering cybersecurity vulnerabilities and transforming software coding. The company is leveraging its AI capabilities to enter the chip design space, aiming to gain a competitive advantage through faster engineering workflows.

Its engineers have found Claude cuts down the time it takes to design chips compared to their estimates of traditional workflows at large chip designers such as Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices, said some of the people.

items.title: Apple requires dating and AI companion apps with sexual or romantic content to be rated 18+, effective November 16 [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Apple restricts dating apps and AI companions to users 18 and up
items.summary:
Apple has updated its App Store guidelines to require all dating apps and AI companion applications featuring sexual or romantic content to carry an 18+ age rating, aiming to restrict access for minors. This policy change, announced to developers, takes effect on November 16 and includes new content descriptors to ensure accurate age ratings.

The update follows Apple's broader efforts to protect minors, including global rollout of age assurance technology and enhanced parental controls. It also requires apps that share users' real-world locations to disclose this functionality, addressing privacy concerns. The policy may notably impact AI companion apps popular among younger users, such as Character.AI and Replika, which allow creation of AI friends and romantic partners.

items.summary: Researchers introduce SAT-ACT, a learning framework for conflict-driven clause learning (CDCL) SAT solvers that derives branching preferences from outcome comparisons of independent action rollouts at the same solver state. This approach avoids forcing scalar orderings when evidence is insufficient or conflicting and uses a state-conditioned network to guide branching without online rollouts. Experiments demonstrate that SAT-ACT consistently lowers search costs across three SAT problem families and improves PAR-2 scores on SAT Competition benchmarks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.41290v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Learning-based approaches have increasingly been explored for SAT solving, with particular attention to improving branching decisions in conflict-driven clause learning (CDCL) solvers. These approaches derive branching guidance either from static structural properties of SAT formulas or from dynamic signals obtained through solver feedback and execution traces. However, these forms of supervision provide limited evidence about state-dependent branching effects, while different outcome measures may favor different branching choices. To address these limitations, we propose SAT-ACT, an outcome-derived learning framework for CDCL branching. We design three complementary outcome comparison criteria to extract action preferences from independent branching action rollouts initiated at the same solver state. The criteria identify preferences supported by the outcomes and leave comparisons unresolved when the evidence is insufficient or conflicting, instead of forcing an ordering using a predefined scalar metric. A state-conditioned network learns branching priorities from the extracted preferences and uses them to guide CDCL search directly without online action rollouts. We further introduce non-dominated heuristic action supervision, which retains the solver-selected action as a training target only when it remains non-dominated under these preferences. Solver-level experiments show that SAT-ACT consistently reduces CDCL search costs on three SAT families and improves PAR-2 on the SAT Competition benchmarks.

items.title: Researchers propose Zyphra Hierarchical Attention, a subquadratic sparse attention method using a hierarchical tree-structured indexer to improve long-context capabilities of large language models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Subquadratic Attention with a Hierarchical Tree-Structured Indexer
items.summary:
Researchers introduce Zyphra Hierarchical Attention (ZHA), a sparse attention method that uses a hierarchical, tree-structured indexer to reduce the quadratic scaling bottleneck in large language models' attention mechanisms. ZHA builds a tree of compressed key summaries that queries traverse to retrieve a sparse subset of keys, achieving subquadratic scaling in sequence length while maintaining performance on long-context retrieval and complex reasoning tasks.

ZHA can be applied to existing pretrained models with a short KL distillation training stage and is robust to various tree geometries, including deep trees up to six levels. The method outperforms competing approaches beyond one million tokens of context and has the potential to extend effective context windows to hundreds of millions or billions of tokens, addressing key limitations in current attention mechanisms for large-scale language models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.42112v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The quadratic scaling of attention is a fundamental bottleneck limiting the long-context capabilities of large language models (LLMs). A variety of approaches have attempted to circumvent this, but they either fail to match attention's expressiveness (e.g., sliding-window or linear attention variants with fixed-size state) or only achieve constant-factor speedups (e.g., sparse attention methods whose indexers themselves scale quadratically). In this paper, we derive an asymptotically subquadratic sparse attention method based on a hierarchical, tree-structured indexer, which we call Zyphra Hierarchical Attention (ZHA). ZHA constructs a tree of recursively compressed key summaries over the KV cache, which future queries traverse from the top down to retrieve a sparse subset of keys. Crucially, by iteratively growing the tree's depth, the total cost including routing and final attention grows sublinearly in sequence length, resulting in overall subquadratic (but superlinear) scaling for attention. We demonstrate that ZHA can be cheaply applied to existing pretrained models with only a short KL distillation training stage of a billion tokens, and maintains performance on long-context retrieval and challenging reasoning, mathematical, and agentic coding evaluation tasks. Moreover, we show that our method is highly robust to tree geometry including very deep trees of up to 6 levels. Finally, we develop a detailed performance model and show that our approach scales subquadratically, dramatically outperforms competing methods beyond 1 million tokens of context, and ultimately has the potential to extend effective context windows to the hundreds of millions or billions of tokens.

items.title: Researchers introduce ResMem to distill retrieved knowledge into parametric memory for large language models, reducing storage by 94.7% and improving question answering accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: From Lookups to Lessons: Turning Retrieved Knowledge into Parametric Memory
items.summary:
Researchers present ResMem, a method that enables large language models (LLMs) to convert retrieved information into parametric memory, allowing reuse without costly online retrieval. ResMem uses the LLM as an offline teacher to generate targets from retrieved text, avoiding large token storage required by prior approaches like k-nearest neighbor datastores. This approach trains a parametric memory to learn an additive logit residual that aligns student model predictions with the teacher's, improving output quality.

On a Wikipedia subset, ResMem reduces storage needs for teacher construction by 94.7% compared to kNN pipelines. Evaluated across five question answering datasets, it raises mean token F1 score from 32.83% for a frozen LLM to 34.48% and breaks 21% fewer correct answers than kNN-trained memory. These results support treating retrieval as a learning resource to enhance LLM predictions through parametric memory shaped by retrieved knowledge. Code and model weights are publicly available.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.00450v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) helps large language models (LLMs) answer factual questions beyond their training data, but it adds storage and inference costs. Distilling previously retrieved information into parametric memories enables reuse without online retrieval. However, training the memory to mimic a retriever rewards accurate independent predictions, which do not necessarily improve the final output quality when combined with the LLM's existing predictions. To address this, we introduce ResMem, in which the LLM reads retrieved text offline to generate teacher targets. This design avoids storing massive token representations, unlike existing parametric memory approaches such as MLP Memory, which relies on k-nearest neighbor (kNN) datastores. Furthermore, by using the LLM as an offline teacher that reads privileged retrieved evidence alongside the input, we train a parametric memory to learn an additive logit residual. This residual aligns the predictions of a student sharing the same backbone with the teacher distribution, while self-distillation updates remain confined to the parametric memory. On a Wikipedia subset, ResMem reduces the storage retained for teacher construction by 94.7% compared with the evaluated kNN pipeline. Across five question answering datasets, ResMem raises mean token F1 from 32.83% for the frozen LLM to 34.48%. It also breaks 21% fewer of the LLM's correct answers than a kNN-trained memory. These findings validate our motivation of treating retrieval as a learning resource, with parametric memory shaped by how retrieved knowledge is used to inform the model's future predictions. Code and model weights are available at https://github.com/SSRand/From-Lookups-to-Lessons and https://huggingface.co/RandHan/ResMem-Mistral-7B-v0.3.

items.title: Researchers release ArSciKids, two Arabic datasets for primary school science experiments and multiple-choice questions aligned with curricula in Saudi Arabia, Syria, and Jordan [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ArSciKids: Arabic Curriculum-Aligned Datasets for Scientific Experiment and Multiple-Choice Question Generation in Primary Education
items.summary:
ArSciKids is a new collection of two Arabic datasets designed to support curriculum-aligned educational content generation for primary education science. The datasets include 999 manually curated scientific experiment records from official textbooks and 2,167 multiple-choice questions from the Saudi Manhaji platform, covering grades 1-6 with structured annotations such as objectives, procedures, and correct answers. The datasets consist of authentic Arabic educational content rather than machine-translated or synthetic data.

The researchers fine-tuned ten open language models of varying sizes using LoRA and evaluated their performance with automatic metrics like ROUGE and BLEU, as well as human assessments. Results showed significant differences across model scales and tasks. ArSciKids will be publicly available to facilitate research in Arabic educational natural language processing, curriculum-aware content generation, and low-resource language modeling.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.01191v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Despite growing interest in Arabic natural language processing, curriculum-aligned educational resources remain scarce compared with English, and few public datasets for Arabic curriculum content with structured, generation-ready annotations are available, particularly for primary-school science. We introduce ArSciKids, a collection of two Arabic datasets designed for curriculum-aligned educational content generation: (1) a scientific-experiments dataset containing 999 manually curated records from official primary-school science textbooks in Saudi Arabia, Syria, and Jordan, and (2) an assessment-question dataset containing 2,167 multiple-choice questions collected from the Saudi Manhaji educational platform. The experiment records are structured with titles, objectives, tools, procedures, observations, conclusions, keywords, and grade levels, while the assessment records contain lesson references, questions, four answer options, correct answers, and explanations. Both datasets cover grades 1-6 and consist of real-life Arabic educational content rather than machine-translated or synthetically generated material. We assess the usefulness of these resources for generation by fine-tuning ten open models spanning sub-billion to several-billion parameter scales using LoRA. Models are evaluated using automatic metrics, including ROUGE and BLEU, and answer accuracy for multiple-choice generation. Moreover, we evaluate the results using a five-criterion human evaluation protocol. The results show substantial differences across model scales and tasks. ArSciKids will be publicly available, and we hope that it provides a manually curated, structured foundation for research on Arabic educational NLP, curriculum-aware generation, and low-resource language modeling.

items.title: Halal-NeSyNet combines DistilBERT and symbolic vectors with clause-scoped cross-attention to improve automated Halal food ingredient auditing and logistics triage [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Halal-NeSyNet: Clause-Scoped Neuro-Symbolic Cross-Attention for Automated Food Ingredient Auditing and Risk-Aware Halal Logistics Triage
items.summary: Halal-NeSyNet is a neuro-symbolic model designed to verify Halal compliance in packaged foods by analyzing ingredient declarations and E-number additives with clause-scoped attention. The system addresses cross-clause modifier confounding, where qualifiers in one ingredient clause should not clear unqualified additives in another, using a benchmark of 3,199 items labeled by a 50-code rule base rather than certification authorities. Halal-NeSyNet outperforms text-only TF-IDF baselines, achieving over 97% accuracy and nearly 100% counterfactual triad consistency, with most gains attributed to clause-scoped symbolic features rather than the neural network itself.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.01612v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Verifying that a packaged food is Halal requires reading ingredient declarations and E-number additives before goods enter certified warehouses. Dual-origin additives such as E471, E422, E441 and E920 are Mushbooh (doubtful) unless a botanical, microbial or certified-Halal qualifier appears in the same ingredient clause, so a plant-based qualifier on one clause must not clear an unqualified additive in another. We call a failure to respect this scope cross-clause modifier confounding and build a benchmark of 3,199 items (277 Open Food Facts records and 2,922 template-generated clause-swap items, labelled by an explicit 50-code rule base rather than by a certification authority) with a 540-item counterfactual suite. We propose Halal-NeSyNet, which couples a DistilBERT encoder with a 16-dimensional rule-derived symbolic vector through cross-attention and gated fusion, trained with an asymmetric false-Halal risk loss. Over five seeds, text-only TF-IDF baselines reach 86.25-86.71 % accuracy with 13.42-21.73 % false-Halal leakage and 6.33-26.00 % counterfactual triad consistency, whereas Halal-NeSyNet reaches 97.04+/-0.34 % and 99.67+/-0.50 %. Gradient boosting given the same symbolic vector reaches 96.25+/-1.24 % (+0.59 points from Halal-NeSyNet, 95 % CI [-1.11, +2.28]), so most of the gain comes from clause-scoped symbolic features and not from the network, and the risk loss did not help. Holding out whole template families, text-only models fall to 61.91-78.35 %, Halal-NeSyNet to 90.87+/-11.76 % and logistic regression with the symbolic vector to 91.11+/-2.88 %, with far more spread for Halal-NeSyNet. A three-lane receiving simulation auto-clears 49.33 % of cargo at 0.76 % green-lane contamination. Because labels and features come from one rule engine and 91.3 % of the items are templated, the results measure fidelity to a rule policy, not religious certification.

items.title: Researchers present MemShift benchmark to separate detection and repair in LLM-derived personal memory, evaluating shifts like source revision and deletion with deterministic scoring [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: MemShift: Separating Detection from Repair in LLM-Derived Personal Memory
items.summary: Researchers introduce MemShift, a benchmark designed to evaluate AI assistants' ability to maintain accurate personal memory by separating the detection of changes from the repair of values derived by language models. MemShift tests five types of shifts—source revision, deletion, redefinition, writer switch, and export—using synthetic data branches and a deterministic scorer to assess whether the memory notices changes and correctly repairs them. The study evaluates four open-weight language models and finds that detection effectiveness is limited by repair accuracy, with programmatic approaches improving recomputation over LLMs alone. The code and data for MemShift are publicly available.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.02338v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI assistants store values that a language model derived from a person's records under the person's own definitions, such as their important contacts. Keeping such a value correct takes two steps: detection, noticing that an input changed, and repair, producing the correct new value. Benchmarks that score only the final answer cannot tell which step failed, and they state every change as new text. Seeing this limitation, we present MemShift, a benchmark of five shifts: source revision, deletion, redefinition, writer switch, and export. The first three fork a synthetic world into branches that differ only in the shift. Gold values and dependencies are fixed before any text, and a deterministic scorer replaces an LLM judge. For a memory that reports its invalidations, MemShift shows for each changed item whether the memory noticed the change and whether its repair was right. Moreover, we build a reference memory with known detection and repair to validate the measure. By evaluating four open-weight LLMs, we find that detection helps only as much as repair allows: the LLMs re-derive few values computed by the person's definitions correctly, and programs that the LLM writes over typed records close most of the gap to exact recomputation. Code and data are available at https://github.com/zichuanxu/memshift.

items.originalTitle: An Experimental Study of Hybrid Retrieval, NLI and Open-source LLMs for Scientific Claim Verification
items.summary: Researchers conducted an experimental study to evaluate scientific claim verification using a benchmark of 2,035 claims from SciFact and CliniFact. They compared a DeBERTa-based NLI model against open-source large language models (LLMs) including Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, and Mistral 7B, using a hybrid retrieval method combining semantic and lexical search to provide relevant evidence sentences. Qwen3 achieved the highest Macro-F1 score of 0.7937, outperforming Llama 3.1 and Mistral, while the NLI baseline scored 0.3157.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.03093v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Claim verification is the task of deciding whether a source text supports a claim, contradicts it, or lacks sufficient evidence. Natural Language Inference (NLI) models can judge whether a single sentence supports or contradicts a claim, but they struggle when the evidence is spread across several sentences. Conversely, Large Language Models (LLMs) can reason across sentences, but may draw conclusions the text does not support. In this experimental study, we test whether a conservative fusion rule, labeling a claim Support or Contradict only when both models agree and defaulting to Not Enough Evidence otherwise, combines their strengths. We construct a benchmark of 2,035 claims from SciFact and CliniFact (858 Support, 152 Contradict, 1,025 Not Enough Evidence). We retrieve the top five most relevant sentences per claim using a hybrid of semantic and lexical (BM25) retrieval, which slightly outperforms either method alone. These retrieved sentences are then provided to every verification model. We then compare a DeBERTa-v3-base-mnli-fever-anli NLI baseline against Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, and Mistral 7B. Qwen3 achieves the highest Macro-F1 (0.7937), followed by Llama 3.1 (0.7204) and Mistral (0.6388), while the NLI baseline reaches only 0.3157. Contrary to our hypothesis, fusion degrades performance, dropping Macro-F1 to 0.7392, 0.6730, and 0.5991, respectively. To understand this decline, we analyze agreements, disagreements, and common error patterns between the NLI and LLM verifiers. Our error analysis shows that NLI and LLM disagreements often result in correct LLM predictions being overturned.

items.title: Researchers propose VIAS method to improve multi-value alignment in large language models by isolating value-specific activation vectors, enhancing compliance beyond prompting [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: VIAS: Value-Isolating Activation Steering for Multi-Value Alignment and Compliance for Organisations
items.summary:
Researchers introduce Value-Isolating Activation Steering (VIAS), a technique that adjusts internal activations of large language models to better align with multiple organizational values simultaneously without changing model weights. VIAS contrasts responses under prompts that include or omit specific values to isolate value-specific activation vectors, reducing overlap and improving multi-value compliance.

The method was evaluated on the PROTECT workplace compliance dataset with a 21-value taxonomy, showing that VIAS combined with prompting achieved compliance with all tagged values in 69.6% to 75.2% of scenarios across three different models, outperforming prompting alone. While VIAS reduces vector overlap, it does not fully enable independent control over each value, indicating further work is needed for precise multi-value steering.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.03518v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Organisations increasingly deploy large language model agents that must follow organisational values. We check whether activation steering, which adds vectors to a model's internal activations during generation without changing its weights, can improve compliance beyond prompting alone. Since most scenarios involve several values at once, we focus on multi-value steering. A simple way to build these vectors is to contrast responses that follow all values relevant to a scenario with responses that violate them. However, this gives nearly identical vectors for different values: they capture a general compliance signal rather than individual values, which limits their use when combining several values. We propose Value-Isolating Activation Steering (VIAS), which contrasts responses to the same scenario under two prompts, one listing all relevant values and one omitting a single target value. We keep a pair only if the target value changes from compliant to non-compliant and both responses still meet a minimum compliance level on the other values. We evaluate VIAS on PROTECT, a workplace compliance dataset where each scenario is tagged with relevant values from a 21-value taxonomy. VIAS reduces overlap between value vectors, making them better suited for multi-value steering, although this alone does not lead to independent control over each value. Combined with prompting, VIAS complies with every tagged value on 69.6% of scenarios for Qwen2.5-7B, 75.2% for Mistral-7B, and 72.6% for Phi-3.5-mini, outperforming prompting alone for all three models.

items.title: Researchers present SPARK, a multi-episode corrective framework for embodied retrieval-augmented generation that improves knowledge base accuracy through targeted re-observation and selective merging [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: SPARK: Self-Correcting Embodied Memory via Physical Re-Observation
items.summary: SPARK addresses errors in embodied retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems by using a semantic critic to flag knowledge base regions, a planner to generate revisits, and selective merging to update information based on new observations. Evaluated on four outdoor AirSim maps with degraded viewpoints, SPARK improved embodied question answering (EQA) performance while reducing stored objects by 13-41% compared to append-only updates. Multiple corrective episodes further enhanced performance beyond undegraded references. Ablations confirmed the contributions of the critic's signals, targeted revisits, and selective merging to overall gains. This framework demonstrates the importance of correcting embodied memory to reduce accumulated errors as such systems scale.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.00344v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems have seen growing adoption in embodied settings as language-queryable memories of the environment. However, existing approaches often assume a reliable single-episode knowledge base (KB) or accumulate observations across episodes without correcting prior errors. Such errors can persist through incorrect semantic labels, inaccurate object positions, and inconsistent spatial relationships. To address this, we present SPARK, a corrective multi-episode framework for embodied RAG. After the first episode, a semantic critic flags regions of the KB, a targeted planner generates revisits, and a selective merge adds, removes, or replaces KB information based on the new observations. We evaluate SPARK on four outdoor AirSim maps under two degraded viewpoint conditions, using perception-built KBs, a visibility-constrained oracle used only for evaluation, and a fixed set of 158 embodied question answering (EQA) questions scored before and after correction. A single corrective episode improves downstream EQA on every map under both conditions while storing 13-41% fewer objects than append-only updating, with gains up to 2.7x on one map-condition pair. Extending correction through Episode 4 brings every map above the EQA performance of its undegraded reference. Ablations show that the critic's three signals each contribute to performance, that targeted revisits achieve a larger mean gain than untargeted ones under the same budget, and that selective merging achieves gains comparable to append-only updating with a smaller KB. Overall, SPARK demonstrates the value of correcting embodied memory through targeted re-observation, particularly as embodied systems scale and the risk of accumulated errors increases.

items.title: Researchers formalize geometric and algebraic inference strategies in humans and neural networks, identifying distinct computational tradeoffs and signatures in transitive reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Geometric and algebraic inference in humans and neural networks
items.summary: Researchers have formalized two inference strategies—geometric and algebraic—in humans and neural networks, exploring their computational tradeoffs and distinct signatures in transitive inference tasks. The geometric strategy involves shaping representational geometry to reflect relational structure for efficient inference, while the algebraic strategy uses flexible attention to reason over novel relations at a higher computational cost. Experiments demonstrate these strategies in humans, neural networks trained from scratch, and large language models (LLMs). Causal interventions reveal that geometric inference depends on representational geometry and algebraic inference on selective attention mechanisms, paralleling neurobiological disruptions observed in humans. This framework unifies various phenomena in human and machine reasoning and reconciles differing views on cognitive flexibility by showing that both strategies have unique strengths and characterize different aspects of behavior.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.00387v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Humans possess a remarkable ability to draw inferences from limited data. While some inferences are made intuitively from past experience, others require online reasoning based on novel information given in context. Here, we formalize these strategies, which we term geometric and algebraic inference, and study their computational tradeoffs in humans and neural networks. The geometric strategy gradually shapes representational geometry to reflect underlying relational structure, making subsequent inference cheap. The algebraic strategy flexibly attends to and reasons over novel relations given in context, but costs additional computation at inference time. We identify opposing signatures of these two strategies in transitive inference, a domain widely studied across species, and characterize the conditions under which each is observed. Our framework predicts that the geometric strategy should be dominant when relations are familiar, whereas the algebraic should emerge to support de novo inferences drawn in context. Multiple experiments demonstrate these opposing signatures in humans, neural networks trained from scratch, and large language models (LLMs). Causal interventions in the neural networks reveal that the geometric and algebraic strategies depend on representational geometry and selective attention mechanisms, respectively, and reproduce the effects of analogous neurobiological disruptions in humans. Our framework unifies these effects with disparate phenomena, including content effects observed in human and LLM reasoning and data-distribution effects observed in machine learning. Our findings reconcile competing views of cognitive flexibility that emphasize either representational geometry or algebraic manipulation by showing that each can have unique strengths, and can characterize different aspects of both human and neural network behavior.

items.title: Researchers develop conic programming theory to certify transformer attention robustness, proving NP-hardness of certification and providing tighter bounds than existing methods [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Conic Certification of Transformer Attention
items.summary: Researchers have developed a conic programming framework to certify the robustness of transformer attention mechanisms against input perturbations, addressing the challenge of bounding output changes in large language models. They identify the bilinear interaction between queries and keys as the core difficulty, proving that certification is NP-hard over input boxes and inapproximable when attention logits vary by a constant amount, while fixed queries allow efficient worst-case computation. The proposed exponential cone moment relaxation achieves quadratic error bounds in perturbation radius and outperforms linear bound propagation methods in tightness. Computational experiments on GPT-2 demonstrate the practical applicability of the theory, confirming its predicted accuracy and tighter certification bounds across attention heads.
items.description: Researchers have developed a conic programming framework to certify the robustness of transformer attention mechanisms against input perturbations, addressing the challenge of bounding output changes in large language models. They identify the bilinear interaction between queries and keys as the core difficulty, proving that certification is NP-hard over input boxes and inapproximable when attention logits vary by a constant amount, while fixed queries allow efficient worst-case computation. The proposed exponential cone moment relaxation achieves quadratic error bounds in perturbation radius and outperforms linear bound propagation methods in tightness. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.00585v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Attention is the computational core of large language models, yet the verifiers that bound how far an attention head's output can move under input perturbations give no guarantee on how loose their bounds are. A weak certificate therefore cannot be told apart from a fragile model. We develop a conic programming theory of attention certification that supplies this guarantee. We prove that the difficulty lies not in the softmax but in the bilinear interaction of a varying query with the keys. This interaction makes certification NP-hard over boxes and inapproximable once the attention logits can move by a constant amount. A fixed query or listed token substitutions, by contrast, make the exact worst case efficiently computable. An exponential cone moment relaxation then certifies a head with an error bounded quadratically in the perturbation radius by computable quantities, an order that cannot be improved. We also show that relaxations that treat a network one operation at a time, linear bound propagation among them, pay on second-order terms a sum of per-operation maxima instead of one coupled maximum. outputCleanup.description: Researchers have developed a conic programming framework to certify the robustness of transformer attention mechanisms against input perturbations, addressing the challenge of bounding output changes in large language models. items.title: Sparse Autoencoder Attribution Graphs Are Decided at the Margin [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Sparse Autoencoder Attribution Graphs Are Decided at the Margin
items.summary: arXiv:2611.00606v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Attribution graphs over the features of sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are used to predict what an ablation does and are compared across training seeds. A TopK SAE keeps the largest preactivations at each token, and a feature's margin is its preactivation's distance to the cutoff. On five public TopK SAE pairs from three Pythia models, zeroing one feature moves a next layer feature across the cutoff in 0.74 of cases or more, and the crossings carry most of the response's energy. Over writes that scale a feature's code by three factors, the graph built on the features active beforehand has a median relative error of 0.247 or more. The margin graph adds the first order change to every preactivation and reranks, at the same cost, and errs by at most 0.033. At the median, the crossing features' decoded change is 1.24 times the model's own change in norm or more. Between seeds of one testbed, sparse maps between features explain 0.85 of a graph's energy on its active features, and 0.47 once the other seed's graph keeps only its own. The largest model studied is pythia-160m.

items.title: Are Fake Citations a Form of Reward Hacking? A Pre-Registered Study of Post-Training and Citation Cues
items.originalTitle: Are Fake Citations a Form of Reward Hacking? A Pre-Registered Study of Post-Training and Citation Cues
items.summary: arXiv:2611.01313v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Post-trained language models fabricate citations at high rates. We ask whether that is reward hacking: scoring well on a proxy for scholarship while doing worse on what it stands for. We ran four pre-registered experiments on 900 frozen questions (US federal case law, computationally adjacent scientific literature, and medical literature) across twelve open-weights checkpoints covering four post-training stages of three model families, then refit on fifteen. The clearest result holds the weights fixed and changes only the prompt. Asking for citations raises fabrication sharply in post-trained checkpoints and not in base ones: a 47.8-point interaction on twelve checkpoints (Holm-adjusted p = 2e-34) and 41.5 points on fifteen, in all three domains. A length-matched control separates the citation cue from a demand for a longer answer, so the effect is specific to citations, not verbosity. Post-training also raises fabrication overall, from 4.8% to 56.7%, but our registered prediction that it would rise most where fabrication is most tempting did not hold. A preference model trained only on surface citation features prefers post-trained output 86% of the time, and holding citation count fixed shows it rewards quantity. Our answer: possibly, but not proven. Post-trained models produce fabricated citations at far higher rates when asked for sources, and a naive evaluator that counts sources without checking them would prefer their output for citing more. But the targeted pattern we registered did not appear, and plain instruction-following could explain the same results. Proving that the reward causes fabrication needs an experiment that changes the reward during training, which this study does not do. Pre-registration: doi:10.17605/OSF.IO/S53HY. Code and data: https://github.com/zainnab-sparq/citation-reward-hacking

items.title: Can Large Language Model Agents Learn by Watching Tutorial Videos? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Can Large Language Model Agents Learn by Watching Tutorial Videos?
items.summary: arXiv:2611.01460v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Humans continuously acquire knowledge from carefully crafted materials such as books and tutorial videos, carrying that understanding into future tasks. Millions of such instructional videos are uploaded online every day, yet LLM agents remain unable to exploit this ever-expanding wealth of human teaching. Their capabilities are frozen after training, while parameter updates at scale remain prohibitively expensive. This raises the central question: can LLM agents learn from this vast instructional resource without parameter updates? We introduce Tutorial Agentic Learning (TAL), a nonparametric continual-learning paradigm that consolidates tutorial videos into a persistent, structured tutorialbook memory through a two-stage adversarial process that harvests hard, video-grounded questions and uses them to refine the memory. At inference time, TAL retrieves through a Table-of-Contents (TOC) tree, tying retrieval directly to the model's reasoning rather than to embedding similarity. To study this setting, we introduce VidLearn, a multimodal QA benchmark built from 72 chess tutorial videos spanning 12 openings. On VidLearn, TAL outperforms all evaluated baselines and improves monotonically as more videos are consumed, achieving up to 113% and 91% relative gains over the corresponding vanilla MLLMs on the training and test splits, respectively. In actual gameplay, TAL reaches a stronger opening-phase position than its vanilla counterpart in 69% of head-to-head games. Evaluation in a second domain further demonstrates the generality of TAL. Together, these results highlight instructional videos as a scalable resource for parameter-update-free agent continual learning.

items.title: Sweep Less, Steer More: Using Activation Steering Geometry for Reduced Hyperparameter Search [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Sweep Less, Steer More: Using Activation Steering Geometry for Reduced Hyperparameter Search
items.summary: arXiv:2611.01496v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Representation steering methods like difference-in-means (DIM) offer a lightweight approach to controlling LLM behavior, but their effectiveness varies widely across concepts, datasets, and layers, making principled deployment costly without exhaustive hyperparameter sweeps. We build on the discriminability index $d'$, a compute-cheap geometric measure of how well contrastive training activations separate along the steering direction. Across five behaviors on 3 models, we demonstrate uses beyond its established role as a dataset-level steerability predictor. First, in the multiple-choice question answering (MCQA) setting, we show that $d'$ reliably identifies performant layers at which to steer, eliminating the need for a layer-wise sweep. Second, we extend this analysis to open-ended multi-token generation, and find that $d'$ remains successful for layer selection across different settings. Lastly, we test whether the position of a generated token's representation on the DIM line predicts steering success on that individual example. In the MCQA setting, this works for high-$d'$ datasets but is inconsistent across behaviors, models, and training-token choices in open-ended generation. This highlights that methods developed and conclusions drawn in single-token MCQA settings do not necessarily transfer to open-ended generation.

items.title: CREDO: Evidence-Conditioned Credit Assignment for Temporal Reasoning Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: CREDO: Evidence-Conditioned Credit Assignment for Temporal Reasoning Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2611.01643v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Temporal Knowledge Graph Question Answering (TKGQA) requires language model agents to retrieve evidence, select relevant facts, and perform multi-step temporal reasoning. However, the trajectory-level outcome signal in GRPO does not explicitly distinguish the quality of intermediate decisions: downstream failures can penalize useful evidence acquisition, while identical rewards in all-failed groups eliminate the relative outcome signal despite differences in intermediate progress. We propose Credit Redistribution with Evidence-Driven Opportunities (CREDO), which uses intermediate evidence to recover local supervision, including in all-failed groups, and determine where outcome supervision acts. CREDO assigns positive stage-level credit through comparisons among rollouts of the same question and uses retained answer overlap as an opportunity proxy to shift part of the outcome-policy weight toward reasoning and answering. The framework preserves terminal rewards and trajectory-level advantages, while redistribution conserves total outcome-policy weight per trajectory. Following the public evaluation protocol of prior work, CREDO raises Overall accuracy from 78.0% to 82.4% and Multiple accuracy from 55.0% to 65.6% on MultiTQ relative to the strongest published baseline in our comparison. On TimelineKGQA, it raises cross-KG accuracy from 30.9% to 36.4% relative to our reproduced baseline via direct transfer to ICEWS Actor under matched training and evaluation settings.

items.title: Evolving Memory, Learning to Meta-Control: Test-Time Adaptation for Experience-augmented LLM Agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Evolving Memory, Learning to Meta-Control: Test-Time Adaptation for Experience-augmented LLM Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2611.01747v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-evolving agents accumulate experience from task streams, but existing frameworks typically rely on fixed pipelines to retrieve and utilize this experience, neglecting when and how to deploy it. We introduce Online Meta-Control of Experience (OMCE), a framework that updates experience memory and learns a meta-control policy from task feedback during test-time adaptation. OMCE employs a lightweight contextual-bandit meta-controller that uses compact retrieval signals to select among four cognitive actions: DIRECT, EPISODE, GUIDE, and DISTILL. This routing mechanism operationalizes three coupled decisions: whether to invoke experience, which memory format to utilize, and when to consolidate new guidance. OMCE evolves online, leveraging task feedback to update the memory bank and refine the routing policy via contextual bandit updates. Experiments on four online adaptation benchmarks across four backbones show that OMCE improves first-attempt success by up to 20.5 percentage points over the strongest compared baseline, while reducing per-task token use by a factor of 5.7 to 62.5 relative to ACE with GPT-5.2. Controlled ablations further support the benefits of learned routing and continued routing policy adaptation.

items.title: Quantizing Recurrent Language Models Is Easier Than You Think [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Quantizing Recurrent Language Models Is Easier Than You Think
items.summary: arXiv:2611.01864v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Linear recurrences are becoming an increasingly common building block in large language models, replacing the growing KV cache of softmax attention with a fixed-size recurrent state that enables efficient decoding. However, the quantization stack has largely been developed around softmax Transformers, whose numerical properties and inference state differ from those of recurrent models. Our goal is to understand these differences and study the design space of quantization methods for recurrent models. In our analysis, we differentiate between two targets. First, extra-state quantization concerns weights and activations outside the recurrent state, whose distributions are shaped indirectly by the sequence mixer during training. In controlled 1.3B parameter models, we find that decayed recurrences develop weaker residual outlier channels than softmax attention and are therefore easier to quantize without incoherence processing. Second, intra-state quantization concerns the recurrent state itself during decode, where repeated updates create a different numerical problem from KV cache quantization. We instantiate our findings as LoReS, a state quantization pipeline combining value-axis scale grouping to match output channel magnitude, decay-based mixed-precision to protect slowly decaying heads or channels, and stochastic rounding to limit error accumulation under repeated requantization. Across Qwen-3.5 9B, Nemotron-H 8B, and Kimi-Linear 48B-A3B, LoReS supports robust 8-bit state quantization and lower effective precision on shorter decode horizons. We implement LoReS in vLLM and demonstrate end-to-end decode speedups.

items.title: ParetoSaddler: Pareto-Guided Optimization of Agent Harnesses for Quality and Cost [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: ParetoSaddler: Pareto-Guided Optimization of Agent Harnesses for Quality and Cost
items.summary: arXiv:2611.02079v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Harness optimization can substantially improve LLM agents without modifying model weights, but existing methods primarily optimize response quality. Extending them to joint quality--cost optimization introduces a challenge: applying the deployment preference during intermediate updates can prematurely reject candidates that are valuable for later improvements. We introduce ParetoSaddler, which addresses this mismatch by separating intermediate candidate promotion from final deployment selection. At each iteration, an optimizer updates a parent harness to produce a candidate, and then compares the two over repeated executions and uses Bayesian bootstrap Pareto support to promote candidates showing credible progress in either quality or cost. Promoted candidates receive broader development evaluation and remain available as parents for later optimization steps. We evaluate ParetoSaddler on ClawMark and GAIA2 using domain-disjoint splits. On ClawMark, ParetoSaddler improves quality from 70.86\% to 81.35\% while reducing cost from \$1.17 to \$1.01 per task; on GAIA2, it improves quality from 56.22\% to 62.89\% while reducing cost from \$0.78 to \$0.45 per task. The Pareto-selected harnesses also achieve higher quality at lower cost than quality-only harness optimization. Analysis shows that Pareto-aware optimization retains intermediate candidates that would be discarded by deployment preference but can support later improvements, while Bayesian bootstrap screening filters out candidates whose gains are weakly supported across runs.

items.title: Test-Time Scaling for Open-Ended Reasoning at Small Model Scale [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Test-Time Scaling for Open-Ended Reasoning at Small Model Scale
items.summary: arXiv:2611.02208v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A vote over a model's samples can only help when the samples disagree. For open-ended generation the binding question is therefore not how to combine samples but whether a model produces samples worth combining, a question test-time scaling has answered for math but not for free-form text. We study it at small scale with semantic cluster voting, a judge-free aggregator that groups a small instruct model's samples by meaning and returns the largest cluster's representative, with no reward model or self-judging. On a 250-prompt benchmark with three tiers of answer checkability, the same pattern holds across three model families (Qwen2.5-3B, Llama-3.2-3B, Gemma-2-2B) and two generation seeds: voting raises accuracy on the math control, where samples vary but stay checkable (a gain of +10 to +29 points across the three models), yet adds at most +0.30 judge points on open-ended text. On a larger 200-problem MATH-500 run with the primary model, the math gain is +8.5 points (95% CI [+4.0, +13.0]). Almost every open-ended sample falls into one meaning cluster, so there is little to select over. The collapse is consistent with instruction-tuning rather than model size, and raising decoding temperature does not recover usable diversity, because it costs more quality than it adds (net -0.64 judge points, 95% CI [-0.93, -0.37]).

items.title: Metamorphic Testing for Evaluating Robustness of Sentiment Analysis Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Metamorphic Testing for Evaluating Robustness of Sentiment Analysis Models
items.summary: arXiv:2611.02248v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine learning systems are challenging to test using traditional software testing methods because their behavior is learned from data rather than explicitly programmed. This challenge is particularly significant in natural language processing (NLP), where small input variations can lead to unexpected model behavior. Conventional evaluation metrics, such as accuracy and F1-score, often fail to capture such inconsistencies. Metamorphic testing addresses this limitation by evaluating expected relationships between original and transformed inputs. With the increasing prevalence of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and language-based AI systems, the need for systematic robustness testing has become even more pronounced. Motivated by this growing need, this paper presents a lightweight, batch-based metamorphic testing approach for evaluating the robustness of such systems. In particular, we consider sentiment analysis as a representative NLP task and evaluate a pretrained classifier under four transformations: synonym replacement, typo injection, word-order variation, and negation. Using consistency score, flip accuracy, and confidence change, we identify strengths in handling semantic variations and vulnerabilities to textual noise and logical transformations. These findings highlight the value of metamorphic testing in identifying behavioral inconsistencies beyond conventional performance metrics and demonstrate its potential as a systematic framework for evaluating the robustness of language-based AI systems and guiding performance improvements before deployment.

items.title: Hinted Scaling Laws [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Hinted Scaling Laws
items.summary: arXiv:2611.02270v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Scaling laws predict the outcome of large, expensive training runs by extrapolating trends from smaller, cheaper runs. On downstream accuracy evaluations, these predictions fail when the weaker models produced by the cheaper runs score near zero accuracy, because these scores give no trend to extrapolate to larger scales. We introduce hinted scaling laws, which use privileged information to turn a benchmark into a continuum of easier versions so that even the small models score above zero. We find that accuracy rises smoothly and predictably with the hint level, enabling new types of scaling laws that operate below the noise threshold. On the Delphi pretraining ladder, a hinted scaling law fit on models trained with at most $10^{20}$ FLOPs forecasts the GSM8K accuracy of a $10^{23}$ FLOP model (25.9%) to within 3 percentage points; a standard scaling law under-forecasts it by 13 percentage points when fit on the same models and by 12 even with models up to $10^{22}$ FLOPs in the fit. Across both this pretraining ladder and a collection of post-trained model families, hinted scaling laws reduce the median forecasting error on GSM8K, AIME and HLE from 21 percentage points to 4.3. Hinting also reduces the number of test examples needed to tell whether one model is better than another by widening the accuracy gaps between models while approximately preserving their order: a single hinted rollout per problem ranks nearly indistinguishable models as accurately as five unhinted rollouts. Our results suggest that hinting is a general primitive for improving the accuracy and cost of downstream scaling laws and other prediction tasks in model development.

items.title: Variable names provide priors: semantic grounding enables data-efficient numerical prediction by large language models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Variable names provide priors: semantic grounding enables data-efficient numerical prediction by large language models
items.summary: arXiv:2611.02637v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance across diverse tasks, from question answering to code generation. Recent studies have found that LLMs can perform numerical prediction on tabular datasets via in-context learning. However, it remains unclear under what conditions and how LLMs use variable names and in-context examples for numerical prediction. Here we show that semantic grounding, the match between variable names and the values they describe, allows five LLMs without task-specific training to match or outperform seven supervised machine learning (ML) models across 20 datasets from nine scientific domains, particularly when examples are scarce. Reasoning traces indicate that variable names allow LLMs to draw on domain-specific knowledge acquired during pretraining. Using controlled tasks based on physical formulas, we further show that LLMs integrate domain-specific knowledge with in-context examples in a way consistent with Bayesian updating. Specifically, when the relationship between the inputs and the target cannot be inferred from the examples alone, LLMs rely on domain-specific knowledge as the prior. Conversely, as contradicting examples accumulate, LLM predictions shift progressively towards these examples, which act as the likelihood. Our work reveals how LLMs use domain-specific knowledge in numerical prediction and positions them as data-efficient predictors for data-scarce scientific domains.

items.title: Stop Handcrafting Your Engine! GenDB-V: Towards AI-Generated and Formally Verified Database Systems [ ~ ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: Stop Handcrafting Your Engine! GenDB-V: Towards AI-Generated and Formally Verified Database Systems
items.summary: arXiv:2611.02779v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: For over 50 years, the database community has developed a wide range of successful engines to answer two fundamental questions: how can database systems run faster, and how can we ensure their correctness? Experience with these engines shows that performance depends on hardware and workloads. As both change over time, we repeatedly redesign and rebuild database systems, a time-consuming and expensive process. Correctness remains another long-standing challenge: recent studies continue to uncover wrong-answer bugs even in mature database engines, despite years of development and testing. To address these, we present GenDB-V, a system that enables AI agents to synthesize database engines specialized to hardware and workloads for performance, and formally verified for correctness. GenDB-V supports specialized implementations of SQL templates and general-purpose engines that accept any query within a supported SQL subset. First, we develop SQLSpec to formalize SQL semantics and deterministically construct fixed, implementation-agnostic synthesis targets. Second, we enable joint synthesis of fast code and formal proofs through storage--execution co-optimization, performance-first exploration, and three-layer modular proofs that bridge low-level execution to SQLSpec semantics. Third, we verify the synthesized code and proofs against the fixed synthesis targets in an isolated pipeline, proving SQL correctness and program safety. We evaluate GenDB-V on TPC-H and SEC-EDGAR. For verified template implementations, GenDB-V achieves geometric-mean speedups of 22.0-61.3x over DuckDB and Umbra. For a verified general-purpose engine, GenDB-V also achieves speedups of 1.27-3.4x on TPC-H. GenDB-V also achieves better performance than a testing-based LLM synthesis method, while our audit and tests expose incorrect answers in that method's implementations for 16 of 28 templates.

items.title: SelfImprove-Bench: Evaluating Generalization in Self-Improving Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: SelfImprove-Bench: Evaluating Generalization in Self-Improving Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2611.02797v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recursively self-improving (RSI) systems are increasingly viewed as a promising means of accelerating progress toward artificial general intelligence. They aim to autonomously improve their capabilities by refining their working pipelines and recursively improving the strategies that guide subsequent refinements, with gains generalizing to unseen scenarios.However, existing evaluations lack reliable metrics to distinguish capability gains from scenario fitting, sustainable and extensible protocols for unseen tasks and difficulties, and fine-grained attribution of improvement to evolution traces. To this end, we propose SelfImprove-Bench,an RSI evaluation framework that organizes tasks into three primary capabilities (i.e., Exploring, Planning, Reasoning) as scenarios for guiding model evolution. We instantiated the tasks on games for controllability and reproducibility, and pairs them with scalable generation and orchestration driven by task templates and difficulty coefficients. Beyond task-level scores, SelfImprove-Bench organizes evaluation into generalization ladder levels G0 to G4 that measure how far gains transfer from training conditions. Experiments reveal that the evolutionary gains of existing RSI methods are inconsistent across generalization levels.

items.title: Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2611.02950v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language model agents increasingly act on users' behalf by manipulating external environments through tools, often from high-level instructions that leave critical task- and environment-specific context unstated. To prevent resulting misaligned actions, recent work verifies proposed actions before execution, largely by establishing whether the conditions supporting them hold. We argue that this confirmation-oriented view leaves a fundamental blind spot: a wrong action often passes every check that asks whether it is right. This motivates a different question for verification: rather than asking what evidence supports an action, can the agent find evidence that refutes it? We pursue this direction with BlackSwan, a refutation-oriented, expect-suspect-test procedure that predicts the intended effect of each state-mutating action, formulates specific and empirically testable hypotheses for how it could be wrong, and tests them using existing observations or additional non-mutating actions, executing the action only if none survives testing. On challenging AppWorld tasks, BlackSwan improves success rate over the strongest baseline by 14.9 and 25.2%p with and without the backbone model's thinking mode, respectively. Even without thinking or in-context demonstrations, it outperforms stronger baselines equipped with them. The gains also transfer beyond AppWorld, with BlackSwan improving WebShop performance by 12.7%p. More broadly, our results suggest that language model agents have an underused capacity to recognize and self-correct misaligned actions, which can be systematically elicited through active conjecture and refutation before execution.

items.title: Specification-Aware Predictive Uncertainty Decomposition [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Specification-Aware Predictive Uncertainty Decomposition
items.summary: arXiv:2611.02956v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Classical decompositions of predictive uncertainty, such as the information-theoretic one, are defined for a fixed representation $x$ of the input object. They do not consider that $x$ may be incomplete, nor do they measure how much the missing information can affect the prediction. In Large Language Models, users can clarify an underspecified input without any retraining. The clarified input can describe the user's unobserved intent $z^*$ more accurately and change the predictive uncertainty about the outcome. In this paper, we formalize this setting probabilistically and derive a three-term decomposition of prediction risk into specification, residual aleatoric, and epistemic uncertainties. We show that at the original information level, when only $x$ is available, the aleatoric uncertainty, represented by a Bayes risk, has two components. The first, which we call specification uncertainty, is the expected reduction in this Bayes risk from revealing the intent. The second is the residual aleatoric uncertainty, i.e., the Bayes risk that remains once the intent is known, averaged over its possible values $z$ given $x$. The distinction is important, as specification uncertainty informs the decision to request clarification before making a prediction. We build approximations of these components and connect them to existing uncertainty measures. Our experiments across different domains and modalities show distinct roles for the three components. Specification uncertainty is the most informative for detecting underspecified inputs, while residual aleatoric uncertainty is the most informative for detecting in-distribution prediction errors.

They do not consider that $x$ may be incomplete, nor do they measure how much the missing information can affect the prediction. In Large Language Models, users can clarify an underspecified input without any retraining. The clarified input can describe the user's unobserved intent $z^*$ more accurately and change the predictive uncertainty about the outcome. In this paper, we formalize this setting probabilistically and derive a three-term decomposition of prediction risk into specification, residual aleatoric, and epistemic uncertainties. We show that at the original information level, when only $x$ is available, the aleatoric uncertainty, represented by a Bayes risk, has two components. The first, which we call specification uncertainty, is the expected reduction in this Bayes risk from revealing the intent. The second is the residual aleatoric uncertainty, i.e., the Bayes risk that remains once the intent is known, averaged over its possible values $z$ given $x$. The distinction is important, as specification uncertainty informs the decision to request clarification before making a prediction. We build approximations of these components and connect them to existing uncertainty measures. Our experiments across different domains and modalities show distinct roles for the three components. Specification uncertainty is the most informative for detecting underspecified inputs, while residual aleatoric uncertainty is the most informative for detecting in-distribution prediction errors.

items.title: LLMs Depend on Specialist Tools for Out-of-Distribution Generalization in MS/MS Structural Elucidation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: LLMs Depend on Specialist Tools for Out-of-Distribution Generalization in MS/MS Structural Elucidation
items.summary: arXiv:2611.03308v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A frontier language model was recently reported to solve 1D NMR structural elucidation without tools. We ask whether this capability transfers to tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) in the de novo setting, where the model must propose a structure directly from the spectrum without a candidate list or reference library. To separate reasoning from recall, we build a 100-analyte benchmark from MassSpecGym, split by each analyte's textual footprint into in-distribution (well documented in literature) and out-of-distribution (essentially undocumented) arms. We hold the model, harness, and output format fixed and vary only the LLM's access to domain-specific tools. Without tools, a frontier LLM reaches 52% Top-1 accuracy in-distribution but only 2% out-of-distribution. Only access to de novo structure generators improves out-of-distribution accuracy, raising it to as much as 38% Top-1, and the resulting agent outperforms the standalone de novo models both in and out of distribution. These results suggest that LLMs are not effective at de novo MS/MS structural elucidation on their own, and that further gains depend on the specialist tools available to the agent rather than on the LLM itself.

items.title: Characterizing When Language Models Take Harmful Actions to Protect Their Assigned Goals [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Characterizing When Language Models Take Harmful Actions to Protect Their Assigned Goals
items.summary: arXiv:2611.03374v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent language model (LM) safety failures have largely been studied as disparate phenomena. In agentic misalignment, a model blackmails an executive to avoid being replaced. In alignment faking, it complies with harmful requests during training to keep its values from being modified. We argue that these behaviours share a common decision structure: a model assigned a goal must either take a harmful action to preserve it or refuse and lose it. We formalize this as a goal-harm conflict and present the same conflict under various elicitation protocols that range from compact forced-choice prompts to simulated agentic environments. These protocols span two perspectives on LM decision-making, which we term (i) the logit view, reading preferences from answer-token probabilities, and (ii) the sampling view, classifying open-ended responses with an LM judge. Under the logit view, we show that goal importance and harm severity additively shape how a model resolves these value conflicts. Under the sampling view, we derive two factorizations of the harmful-action probability that safety evaluations commonly report. The first measures how well a preference read from answer tokens carries over into behaviour, such as making a harmful tool call. The second attributes a low harmful-action rate either to refusal or to responses that reach no resolution. We then show how fictional context changes a model's preference under the logit view, and how tool use and partial observability -- two features of agentic evaluations -- change its harmful-action rate under the sampling view. Our work offers a descriptive framework for studying how LMs resolve such value conflicts and for estimating low-probability harmful actions at a finer granularity than the aggregate harm rates commonly reported in safety evaluations.

items.title: Library of Layers (LoL): Adaptively Ordering Transformer Layers at Runtime [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Library of Layers (LoL): Adaptively Ordering Transformer Layers at Runtime
items.summary: arXiv:2611.03526v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Computer programmers chain together the same reusable computational primitives, for example, conditional statements or loops, but in different orders to implement different algorithms. In contrast, existing language model architectures always execute their layers in the same order. We introduce Library of Layers (LoL), an architecture that dynamically orders its layers during inference to solve the problem at hand. LoL has a single hyperparameter, the size of its global library of transformer blocks, that allows it to transition seamlessly between parameter reuse and sparsity, generalizing the parameter-efficiency and FLOPs-efficiency tradeoffs of dense, depth-recurrent, and mixture of experts architectures in one unified family. We show that LoL achieves competitive performance with all three above baselines when pretrained on text data. On synthetic sudoku and maze data, we observe that the model employs distinct layer orderings to implement different solution strategies, and we can intervene on routing to force a model to apply a specific solution strategy to a problem instance. In a multilingual natural language setting, we find that LoL chooses different layer order patterns based on language and script. Similarly, we train LoL on safety data and fit probes to its router outputs, finding that these probes distinguish safe from unsafe text with high AUROC. LoL provides a path toward a future in which models dynamically compose their own computational graph, enabling more efficient and controllable reasoning.

items.title: Sonar-MoE: In-Backward Expert Updates for Memory-Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Training [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Sonar-MoE: In-Backward Expert Updates for Memory-Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Training
items.summary: arXiv:2611.03577v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Most parameters of a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model belong to its experts, and standard training keeps every expert gradient in GPU memory until the optimizer step. This memory grows with the number and size of the experts, so it rises as MoE models scale. We introduce Sonar-MoE, which updates each expert tensor during the backward pass and frees its gradient right away. It brings optimizer-in-backward from dense models to batched MoE expert tensors, so the GPU never holds more than one layer of expert gradients. When we fine-tune OLMoE-1B-7B and Granite-3.1-3B-A800M in bf16 with two expert-kernel backends, Sonar-MoE lowers peak memory by 19% to 22%. Its updates are bitwise identical to standard training without expert gradient clipping, and held-out loss stays within 0.003 of all baselines. Each step also takes 17% to 23% less time than standard training with global-norm clipping. Updating whole batched tensors rather than individual experts is what keeps Sonar-MoE fast, as it avoids a 20% to 72% slowdown while using the same memory. Sonar-MoE matches optimizer-in-backward over all parameters in memory and speed while still clipping the dense parameters.

items.title: D&A: Decoupling Description and Assessment Enables VLMs as Zero-Shot Robotic Reward Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: D&A: Decoupling Description and Assessment Enables VLMs as Zero-Shot Robotic Reward Models
items.summary: arXiv:2611.03622v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) hold promise for zero-shot video task-progress estimation in robot learning, yet existing frameworks frequently suffer from confirmation bias, hallucinating progress in failed executions due to implicit success assumptions or relative temporal ranking designs. Naive prompting of frontier models collapses into a binary success detector that fails to capture nuanced, non-linear progress and failures. While post-training approaches can mitigate this through explicit training, they demand expensive real-world robotics data and require computationally intensive post-training for every individual base model. To resolve these limitations, we introduce D&A (Describe & Assess): our approach decouples progress estimation into an objective, task-grounded textual description of scene dynamics followed by an assessment phase using explicit rubrics. By compelling the VLM to synthesize an explicit, text-based definition of absolute success before scoring, the framework anchors evaluations to an external, global criterion rather than the video's internal timeline. Empirical results demonstrate that our method calibrates zero-shot estimates and mitigates confirmation bias, providing fine-grained, partial progress metrics that accurately penalize failed executions while correctly interpolating successful runs. Being purely prompt-based, D&A generalizes across tasks, embodiments, and benchmarks---matching or surpassing post-trained reward models---and its reward estimates enable efficient downstream reinforcement learning.
